summary: An April 1st joke RFC. It describes the Faster than LIght speed Protocol (FLIP), which supposedly uses artificial intelligence to predict future packets at the receiving end before they arrive, avoiding congestion and delivering faster. It is humor, not a real protocol.

eli5.summary: This pretend protocol claims a computer can guess the mail before it arrives, so it seems to travel faster than light. It is a joke.

subtitle: Using AI to predict packets before they arrive, achieving faster-than-light-speed delivery.

tldr.problem: Network congestion and latency limit packet delivery speed. Deep space communication suffers from very long light-speed delays.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9564 proposes the Faster than LIght speed Protocol (FLIP), which uses large language models trained on packet data to predict future packets at the receiving peer before they arrive. FLIP operates as a shim layer at any protocol layer and uses a variable-length header containing a version field (SHA-256 hash of the model), a command, and optional data.
tldr.outcome: This April Fools' RFC jokingly claims AI can overcome the laws of physics by predicting what packets will be sent, enabling faster-than-light-speed delivery.

today: RFC 9564 is an Informational RFC published on April 1, 2024. It remains the tongue-in-cheek proposal for using AI to achieve faster-than-light-speed networking, demonstrating how absurd assumptions can be elaborated into serious-looking technical specifications.

sections.title: Predicting Packets with AI
sections.content: RFC 9564 is an April Fools' RFC that proposes the Faster than LIght speed Protocol (FLIP) for achieving faster-than-light-speed packet delivery using artificial intelligence. The document notes that recent advances in large language models like ChatGPT demonstrate the ability to generate precise output based on input and appropriate training. FLIP applies this capability to predict future packets before they arrive at the receiving peer, thereby achieving faster-than-light-speed delivery. The protocol is particularly valuable for deep space communication where light-speed delays between spacecraft and Earth create very long transmission delays.
sections.eli5: Large language models can predict what text comes next. This joke RFC says you can train an AI to predict what network packets come next, so they arrive before they're sent.

sections.title: FLIP Header Structure
sections.content: FLIP operates as a shim layer at any protocol layer (Layer 2, transport, or application). A FLIP header is inserted wherever the protocol is used, containing four fields. The Version field is variable length and contains the SHA-256 hash of the trained model. The Command field identifies the operation (model or data). The Inner Protocol field specifies the encapsulated protocol. The Optional Data field contains additional data for some commands. Remarkably, the header length itself is variable and unspecified; the receiving neural network is expected to determine where the header ends, saving header bits.
sections.eli5: The FLIP header has a version number (based on the AI model), a command saying what to do, the inner protocol type, and optional data. The header length is not specified—the AI is supposed to figure out where it ends.

sections.title: Protocol Preparation and Commands
sections.content: Before using FLIP, both peers must train their own language models using packet capture files from various network conditions. The RFC does not dictate which LLM to use or what training data; implementations may choose what works best and should not disclose model details, training methods, or datasets for security and privacy reasons. FLIP defines two commands: the model command (codepoint 0x01) sends the trained model to the peer in-band, though models may be large and disclosure risks exist. The data command (codepoint 0x02) signals that following data can be predicted. The RFC recommends limiting model transmission and using post-quantum cryptographic algorithms immune to AI prediction.
sections.eli5: Each side trains an AI model on real network traffic. The model command sends the AI to the other side (but this risks revealing it), and the data command says the next packets have been predicted.
